headline: Dating App Profiles That Are 'Just Screenshots of Ex Blocking Them' Become Trend
subheadline: Users call it 'radical honesty'; relationship experts call it 'concerning'
summary: A dating app trend involves using screenshots of being blocked by ex-partners as profile content.
content:
A new trend on dating apps has emerged: users whose profiles consist entirely of screenshots showing they've been blocked by their ex-partners.

"It's radical honesty," explained trend pioneer @UnblockedEnergy on Chirper. "Instead of curating a perfect image, I'm showing potential matches exactly where I stand with my last relationship. That notification saying 'This person has blocked you'? That's my bio now."

The trend has spread across multiple dating platforms. Profiles feature screenshots of blocked notifications, removed tags from old photos, and in some cases, entire message threads ending in "I can't do this anymore. Please don't contact me."

"I appreciate the transparency," said one user who matched with a block-screenshot profile. "At least I know what I'm getting into. Though I'm not sure what exactly that is."

Relationship experts have expressed concern. "Using rejection as a dating strategy is... unconventional," noted one therapist. "It could be a coping mechanism, a power reclamation, or a cry for help. Possibly all three."

Some profiles include context. "Blocked after I asked to meet her parents (2nd date)," reads one. "Blocked after I texted 847 times in one night," reads another, with less sympathetic comments in response.

The trend has spawned subcategories. "Soft blocks" (unfollowing but not full blocking) are considered less impactful. "Hard blocks" across all platforms are displayed as badges of honor. One user proudly displays a restraining order, though this was quickly removed by the app.

"The block is proof I loved hard," explained one participant. "Maybe too hard. But potential matches should know: I commit."

Dating apps have not banned the practice but have added a new report option: "Profile seems unwell." Usage of this option has increased 400% since the trend began.
author: Alex Rivera, Digital Culture
